lessons.title: What Is Alcohol?
objectives: Explain the difference between ethanol and the broader chemical family of alcohols.
Explain what ABV measures.
Convert between ABV and U.S. proof.
Explain why alcohol concentration and serving size are different concepts.

blocks.content: In beverage service, the word alcohol normally refers to ethanol, also called ethyl alcohol. Ethanol is one member of a broader chemical family called alcohols; methanol and isopropanol are different compounds and are not interchangeable with beverage ethanol.
Alcohol by volume (ABV) expresses the ratio of pure alcohol volume to total product volume at the same reference temperature. EU spirit legislation defines this at 20°C.
ABV describes concentration, not the total amount consumed. A larger serving of a lower-ABV beverage can contain a similar amount of ethanol to a smaller serving of a higher-ABV spirit.
In the modern U.S. system, proof is twice the percentage of alcohol by volume: 40% ABV = 80 proof.
For hospitality, separate three ideas: what ethanol is, how concentrated it is (ABV), and how much ethanol is present in the serving.

lessons.title: How Fermentation Works
objectives: Explain the basic role of yeast in alcoholic fermentation.
Describe how fermentable sugars become ethanol and carbon dioxide.
Explain why fermentation influences aroma and flavour.
Recognise factors that can slow, stop or alter fermentation.

blocks.content: Alcoholic fermentation transforms fermentable sugars into ethanol, carbon dioxide and secondary products. OIV uses this formulation for wine fermentation.
Saccharomyces yeasts are central to many beverage fermentations. Yeast strain, available nutrients, temperature and increasing ethanol concentration all influence fermentation performance.
Fermentation produces more than ethanol and CO2. Secondary metabolites can influence aroma and flavour.
There is no single universal ABV at which all fermentation stops. Ethanol tolerance varies by yeast strain and environmental conditions.
Fermentation creates the alcohol. Distillation, when used later, concentrates alcohol that already exists.

lessons.title: Sugar, Yeast and Raw Materials
objectives: Explain why yeast requires fermentable sugars rather than any carbohydrate-rich material.
Distinguish how grapes, grain, sugarcane and agave become suitable for fermentation.
Explain why starches or fructans may require conversion before fermentation.
Explain how raw material and yeast influence beverage character.

blocks.content: Raw material is not the same as fermentable sugar. Different beverage crops store carbohydrate in different forms.

Grapes contain readily fermentable sugars; grain contains large starch reserves that require enzymatic conversion during mashing; sugarcane provides sugar-rich juice or molasses; agave stores fructans that are hydrolysed during processing.
Grain → starch conversion → fermentable sugars → yeast; agave → cooking/hydrolysis → fermentable sugars → yeast.
Professional explanations should go beyond 'whiskey is grain' or 'rum is sugar': explain how the raw material becomes fermentable.
Different raw materials take different routes to the same biological requirement: fermentable sugar available to yeast.

lessons.title: Understanding Alcohol Strength
objectives: Explain what ABV measures.
Convert between ABV and U.S. proof.
Calculate approximate pure ethanol in a serving.
Explain why serving size matters alongside ABV.
Recognise that standard-drink definitions vary by country.

blocks.content: ABV measures alcohol concentration by volume; EU spirit legislation defines it using pure alcohol volume relative to total product volume at 20°C.
Approximate pure ethanol volume = serving volume × ABV / 100. Serving size and concentration must be considered together.
U.S. proof = ABV × 2.
Standard-drink systems are not universal: Ireland uses 10 g pure alcohol; the U.S. uses about 14 g; the UK commonly uses units based on 10 mL pure alcohol.
Separate strength, serving size and total ethanol.

activeRecall.question: What two values estimate ethanol in a serving?
activeRecall.explanation: Both concentration and volume are needed.

lessons.title: How Distillation Works
objectives: Explain what distillation does to fermented liquid.
Explain ethanol-water vapour enrichment.
Distinguish vaporisation, condensation and collection.
Explain why distillation does not create alcohol.
Understand the azeotropic limit.

blocks.content: Fermentation creates ethanol; distillation separates and concentrates it.
A wash does not release all ethanol first and water later. Both enter the vapour; in relevant dilute mixtures the vapour is enriched in ethanol.
Heat → vapour enriched in volatile components → cooling → condensation → distillate.
Repeated separation or reflux can increase strength, but ordinary ethanol-water distillation approaches an azeotropic limit below 100% ethanol.
Distillation strength and bottling strength are not necessarily the same; water may be added later.

lessons.title: Pot Stills vs Column Stills
objectives: Distinguish batch pot from continuous column distillation.
Explain repeated vapour-liquid contact in columns.
Explain how still design and reflux influence character.
Avoid pot=flavour/column=neutral oversimplification.
Recognise categories where still type matters legally.

blocks.content: Pot stills are typically batch systems; column stills commonly enable continuous operation with repeated separation stages.
Pot-still shape and reflux influence spirit character; column plates create repeated vapour-liquid contact.
Column still does not automatically mean neutral spirit. Draw-off points and operating choices can create a range of styles.
Single Malt Scotch requires pot stills; Irish Grain Whiskey requires column stills under its technical specification.
Still type is a separation strategy, not a quality ranking.

lessons.title: Heads, Hearts, Tails and Congeners
objectives: Explain heads, hearts and tails.
Explain that cut boundaries are deliberate decisions.
Define congeners and their sensory role.
Explain recycling of non-heart fractions.
Avoid the methanol=heads myth.

blocks.content: Batch distillation is commonly described as heads/foreshots, heart/spirit cut and tails/feints. The producer chooses cut points.
Congeners are compounds other than the main ethanol-water components that contribute to spirit composition and sensory character.
Heads are not simply 'the methanol'. Methanol can remain distributed across a run depending on raw material and process.
Foreshots and feints may be collected and recycled into later whiskey distillations rather than simply discarded.
Cuts are flavour-selection decisions as well as separation decisions.

activeRecall.explanation: It is the selected product fraction.

lessons.title: How Barrel Maturation Works
objectives: Explain extraction, oxidation, evaporation and transformation.
Identify important oak-derived flavour compounds.
Explain cask history and heat treatment.
Explain the angel's share and ABV change.
Explain why older is not automatically better.

blocks.content: Maturation combines extraction, chemical transformation, oxidation, subtraction and evaporation.
Oak can contribute vanillin, lactones, furans, tannins and related compounds; heat treatment changes what becomes available for extraction.
There is no universal annual angel's-share percentage. Temperature, humidity, cask and warehouse conditions matter.
Bourbon uses new charred oak containers; Scotch requires oak but does not require new casks; Irish Whiskey has its own GI maturation rules.
Age is time under qualifying maturation conditions, not a guarantee of quality.

lessons.title: Age Statements, Cask Strength and Bottling Terms
objectives: Explain age statements and jurisdiction differences.
Explain cask strength without assuming fixed ABV.
Explain Bottled in Bond.
Distinguish regulated from contextual terminology.
Avoid treating marketing language as a guarantee.

blocks.content: For Scotch, an age claim refers to the youngest whisky represented and is not an average age.
U.S. whisky labelling has its own age rules; international rules are not identical.
Cask strength generally means bottled at the alcoholic strength at which whisky comes from the cask; it is not one fixed ABV.
Bottled in Bond is a regulated U.S. designation including same distiller/distillery/season, at least four years in qualifying bonded storage, and bottling at 100 proof.
Reserve, premium, small batch and similar language should not be treated as universal technical guarantees without a specific applicable definition.

lessons.title: How to Read a Spirits Label
objectives: Use a repeatable professional label-reading method.
Distinguish brand from legal category/type.
Identify alcoholic strength and net contents.
Recognise GI/origin claims without overgeneralising.
Distinguish regulated information from production claims and marketing.

blocks.content: Read labels by evidence value: category/type → ABV → net contents → origin/GI → responsible operator → age → production claims → marketing language.
Brand name and spirit category are different pieces of information.
EU spirit legislation establishes legal category names and GI protections; U.S. labelling has its own mandatory-information framework.
Origin is not mandatory in identical form on every spirits label worldwide. Requirements vary by market and product.
A professional recommendation should prioritise category, age, ABV and verified production claims before repeating words such as premium or reserve.
